summary: Retires DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV) and reclassifies RFC 4431 and RFC 5074 as Historic. It also updates RFC 6698 and RFC 6840 so the DLV record and DLV registries are no longer part of certificate matching or trust anchor selection.

plainLanguage.summary: An old backup way to check a phone book is shut down because the main way works now. This document officially says to stop using the backup.

questions: is dnssec lookaside validation still used
what is the dlv record type code
subtitle: The official retirement of DNSSEC Lookaside Validation, a stopgap from when the DNS root was still unsigned.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV) let zones publish trust anchors outside the normal DNS delegation chain, but it had outlived its purpose and only added complexity.
tldr.mechanism: This document moves RFC 4431 and RFC 5074 to Historic status, tells implementers that DLV SHOULD NOT be implemented or deployed, and updates RFC 6698 and RFC 6840 to drop DLV from their text.
tldr.outcome: DLV is retired. The DLV record type (code 32769) is marked Obsolete at IANA, and zones that still relied on DLV are treated as insecure.

today: RFC 8749 is a Proposed Standard that retires DLV and updates RFC 6698 and RFC 6840. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so DLV remains Historic.

sections.title: Why DLV Existed
sections.content:
DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV) was introduced to help DNSSEC get adopted at a time when the root zone and many top-level domains (TLDs) were unsigned. It allowed an entity with a signed zone under an unsigned parent, or one whose registrar did not accept DS records, to publish trust anchors outside the normal DNS delegation chain.

The root zone was signed in July 2010. As of May 2019, 1389 out of 1531 TLDs had a secure delegation from the root. The RFC concludes that DLV has served its purpose and can retire.
sections.plainLanguage: DLV was a side door for people whose parent could not vouch for them yet. Once almost every front door worked, the side door was no longer needed.

sections.title: The Case Against Keeping DLV
sections.content:
The RFC admits that one could argue DLV is still useful, since some TLDs remain unsigned. It lists the costs of keeping it:

  • It reduces the pressure to get the parent zone signed.
  • It reduces the pressure on registrars to accept DS records.
  • It complicates validation code.

Its reach was also limited. Not every validator implemented DLV (only BIND 9 and Unbound did). The one well-known DLV registry, dlv.isc.org, was deprecated on September 30, 2017 and replaced with a signed empty zone. The RFC also notes there are no known uses of DLV for distributing trust anchors in private enterprises.
sections.plainLanguage: The backup phone book made people lazy about fixing the main one, made the system harder to run, and only two kinds of phones could read it anyway. Its only well-known copy had already been emptied.

sections.title: Moving DLV to Historic Status
sections.content:
Two RFCs specify DLV. RFC 4431 defines the DLV resource record, and RFC 5074 defines the mechanism for publishing trust anchors outside the delegation chain and how validators use them. This document moves both to Historic status.

That is a clear signal to implementers that the DLV resource record and the DLV mechanism SHOULD NOT be implemented or deployed.

The RFC also fixes up documents that referred to the retired ones. RFC 4431 is referenced only by RFC 5074. RFC 5074 is referenced by three RFCs, covered next.
sections.plainLanguage: The two rule books about the backup phone book are stamped OLD. Nobody should build or start using it anymore.

sections.title: Effects on RFC 6698, RFC 6840 and RFC 8198
sections.content:
RFC 6698 (DANE TLSA) said that DNSSEC forms certificates by combining a DNSKEY, DS or DLV record with an associated RRSIG record. This document updates it to exclude the DLV resource record from certificates.

RFC 6840 said that when trust anchors come from different sources, a validator may choose between them by their perceived reliability. In practice validators did not do this; BIND 9 and Unbound only offered a DLV trust anchor as a fallback. This document updates RFC 6840 to exclude DLV registries from trust anchor selection.

RFC 8198 (aggressive use of the validated cache) cites RFC 5074 only because aggressive negative caching was first proposed there, so it needs no change.
sections.plainLanguage: Two other rule books mentioned the backup phone book, so each gets a small fix to stop mentioning it. A third only said where an idea came from, so it stays as is.

sections.title: IANA Action
sections.content: IANA updated the annotation of the DLV resource record type, code 32769, to Obsolete in the Domain Name System (DNS) Parameters registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of record types now has a note beside DLV saying it is obsolete.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Once the DLV mechanism is retired, zones that rely on DLV for their validation will be treated as insecure. The RFC judges the chance of this actually happening to be very low, because no well-known DLV registry exists.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone still depended on the backup phone book, they would now be treated as unchecked. That is very unlikely, since the backup book is gone.

items.title: Less signing pressure
items.text: Reduces the pressure to get the parent zone signed.

items.title: Less registrar pressure
items.text: Reduces the pressure on registrars to accept DS records.

items.title: Limited reach
items.text: Only BIND 9 and Unbound implemented DLV.
